p.title: Mathematical Modeling, Analysis and Simulation Utilizing Machine Learning Tools for Assessing the Impact of Climate Lobbying

ext.title: Mathematical Modeling, Analysis and Simulation Utilizing Machine Learning Tools for Assessing the Impact of Climate Lobbying
ext.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.09617v1 [physics.soc-ph], submitted 22 Mar 2025 (manuscript dated May 16, 2025). No journal venue stated in the text.
ext.document_type: arXiv preprint; applied mathematics paper presenting a deterministic compartmental ODE model of congressional voting with lobbying and campaign-donation compartments, one simulated case study, stability analysis, and SVM-based sensitivity analysis.

ext.research_question: Can a compartmental differential-equation model of legislators (not yet introduced, undecided centrists, yes, no), extended with lobbyists, lobbying money, and campaign donations, simulate and predict roll-call passage, and how do lobbying and donations change outcomes? Stated objectives (a) build the model, (b) study how interactions shape legislative behavior, (c) predict likelihood of passage (p.3).
ext.theory: Epidemiology-style mass-action peer influence: undecided legislators (C) move to yes (Y) or no (N) at rates beta_F, beta_A times interactions with Y or N (eqs 2.1a-d, p.4-5). Intro frames lobbying as influence spreading through a network (p.3), but the model itself uses mass action, not a network. Lobbying side: firm value change Delta pi_i = pi*_i - pi0_i; firms with Delta pi > 0 lobby for, < 0 against (Sec 2.1, p.5, following Meng and Rode [17]); lobbying money is split by (1 - psi). Donations drain money M_F, M_A at rates I_F, I_A (eqs 2.2a-h, p.6-7). Authors claim this is the first compartmental-model use of this kind in political science (p.21).
ext.data: Single case: the 2009 ACESA (American Clean Energy and Security Act, called the Waxman-Markey Bill, p.19) House and Senate votes. Unit: individual legislators in compartments. Population: House S = 435, Senate S = 100 (Table 1, p.19). Lobbyist counts: ProPublica Represent database, ACESA-related lobbyists including former federal employees, 2006-2012 (Sec 2.4 p.9; Fig 3 caption p.9), rising from 0 to about 581 in a logistic-like pattern. Campaign money initial values MF = 345,873,085 and MA = 283,377,397 (Table 1). Parameters in Table 2 (p.32-33) are literature-sourced, e.g., alpha_F(H) 0.449, alpha_A(H) 0.382, alpha_C(H) 0.168 [16]; alpha_F(S) 0.41, alpha_A(S) 0.37, alpha_C(S) 0.22 [16]; nu 5.258e-10 [24]; psi 0.47847 [4]; I_F 345873.09 and I_A 283377.340 [17]; beta_F(H)=beta_A(H)=0.00005425 [7]; beta_F(S)=beta_A(S)=0.000437 [7]; L max = 600 [24][11]. No individual-level or survey data. Sensitivity and SVM runs use 1000 samples per figure (p.14-17). N for the empirical comparison: 435 House and 100 Senate members, one bill.
ext.method: Deterministic ODE system. Baseline model (eqs 2.1a-d, p.4-5) and extended model with lobbyists L_F, L_A, money M_F, M_A and donations I_F, I_A (eqs 2.2a-h, p.6-7). Well-posedness: positivity via an invariant-domain lemma stated in the text (p.7-8) and boundedness via M(t) = S + C + Y + N constant (p.8). Stability: linearization about (0, C0, 0, 0) (unstable) and (0, 0, Y0, N0) (stable), in Sec 3.1 (p.10) and Sec 3.2.2 (p.12), with closed-form L_F(t), L_A(t) (Sec 3.2.1, p.11). Simulation: no solver, software or numerical tolerance stated. Sensitivity: 10% variation of centrist-flow parameters with distributions of final C, Y, N (Sec 4, p.12-13); parameter sweeps labelled pass/fail and separated by linear SVM (Sec 4.1-4.2, p.14-17); individual parameter impact ranking (Sec 4.3, Fig 12, p.18-19). Ideology sensitivity via centrist band (Sec 5.3, p.20-21). Validation: compare simulated final House and Senate counts to actual tallies using percent error (Sec 5.1, p.19-20).
ext.identification: None in the econometric sense. No estimation, no quasi-experiment, no causal design. Parameters are fixed from cited literature (Table 2). Validation is a comparison of simulated final vote counts to actual ACESA tallies. The lobbying-on vs lobbying-off contrast (p.19-20) is a simulation contrast under chosen inputs. The abstract says parameters were estimated from public lobbying records and literature, but the text gives no estimation procedure.
ext.scope: Population: US Congress, the House (435 seats) and Senate (100 seats), one bill, ACESA (2009). Era: lobbying counts 2006-2012 (Fig 3, p.9); the House and Senate votes of 2009 (abstract p.1, Sec 5 p.19). Institution: federal legislature. Authors state that the model has been applied to one bill and that a broader bill set is needed (p.23).

key_findings.finding: Baseline House simulation with no lobbying or donations: model settles at yes/no/undecided counts, compared with actual tally.
key_findings.numbers: Model 230 yes, 196 no, 9 undecided vs actual 219 yes, 212 no, 4 abstain; percent error 5.02% (yes), 7.55% (no).

key_findings.finding: Adding campaign donations alone changes almost nothing; authors conclude donations have limited impact on passage.
key_findings.numbers: 231 yes, 196 no, 8 undecided (one undecided legislator moves to yes).

key_findings.finding: Adding lobbying (with donations) moves the House prediction closer to the actual count; authors attribute the shift mainly to lobbying converting undecided legislators.
key_findings.numbers: 231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided; percent error 5.48% (yes), 4.25% (no). Undecided fell from 9 to 1, i.e., 8 legislators resolved in total.

key_findings.finding: Senate baseline and extended runs barely differ; authors say lobbying has minimal effect in the Senate, which they read as consistent with ACESA failing against the 60-vote filibuster threshold.
key_findings.numbers: Baseline 52 yes, 47 no, 1 undecided; with lobbying and donations 52 yes, 48 no, 0 undecided. No Senate actual tally is given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Stability: the all-undecided point is unstable; the point with Y and N positive and S, C at zero is stable, so Y and N converge to positive constants and the legislature tends toward a decision. Same qualitative result holds with lobbying and donations included.
key_findings.numbers: No numeric equilibrium values for Y0 or N0 are reported in the text.

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity to a 10% change in centrist flow parameters: final C, Y, N look roughly normally distributed; trajectories cross the actual House vote count, which authors read as robustness.
key_findings.numbers: Parameters varied by 10%; no summary statistics beyond the figures are given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Parameter-impact ranking: centrist-lobbying parameters (M_LF, M_LA) and tau have substantial influence on outcome; initial compartment sizes (S) have minimal impact.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative ranking only; no effect sizes in the text.

key_findings.finding: SVM pass/fail boundaries: most single-parameter sweeps predict passage; beta and phi matter for passage, tau does not; no clean boundary for the multi-parameter sweeps; authors conclude no simple rate-constant condition guarantees passage.
key_findings.numbers: Linear SVM trained on 1000 samples per figure; red (fail) points lie inside the pass region in Fig 9.

key_findings.finding: Centrist band definition matters: widening the centrist band from -0.25 to 0.25 to -0.35 to 0.35 flips the House result so that no votes exceed yes votes.
key_findings.numbers: Band +/-0.25 vs +/-0.35 on a -1 to 1 ideology scale; the flipped vote counts are not given in the text.

key_findings.finding: ACESA lobbyist counts rise from 0 toward about 581 in a logistic-like pattern over 2006-2012.
key_findings.numbers: Upper bound approximately 581 lobbyists; Table 2 uses L max = 600 (p.33).

key_findings.finding: Introduction context (cited to Meng and Rode [17], not produced by this paper's model): lobbying accounted for 14% of lobbying expenditures in the period, and lobbyists reduced the likelihood of ACESA passage by about 13%.
key_findings.numbers: 14% of lobbying expenditures; about 13% reduction in passage likelihood (cited).

limitations: Single bill (ACESA) with one validation point per chamber; the authors themselves say the model should be applied to a broader set of bills (Sec 6, p.23).

Headline claim vs own numbers: the Introduction says the model predicts roll-call outcomes 'within 5% of the actual results' (p.3). The reported yes errors are 5.02% (baseline, p.19) and 5.48% (lobbying, p.20), and the no error is 7.55% (baseline, p.19). Only the lobbying-case no error (4.25%, p.20) falls within 5%.

Parameters are taken from literature and fixed (Table 2), not estimated from data. The abstract mentions estimating parameters, but the text gives no estimation procedure. Lobbying-money inputs rho_Y, rho_N and the firm-level Delta pi values are not reported, so the M_F and M_A inputs cannot be reproduced from the text.
The framework is deterministic. The authors say real-time data and stochastic elements would improve it (p.18, p.22).
Outcome depends on how centrists are defined (Sec 5.3, p.20-21). The ideology scale source is not named in the text beyond a -1 (liberal) to 1 (conservative) range.
Senate validation is qualitative: no actual Senate tally is reported, and the model's 52-48 result is not compared numerically with the failed filibuster outcome.
The lobbying-vs-donations claim rests on small shifts: 8 undecided legislators in total (9 to 1) out of 435, and donations move one legislator (p.19-20).
Authors note donation effects may reflect legislators' ideology rather than direct influence, citing Bonica [5] (p.20).
SVM section: overlap between pass and fail points is acknowledged (p.16); the SVM dimensionality is given as 2 in captions of Figs 6-8 and 6 in Figs 9-11 (p.14-17) with no sampling method described.
Positivity relies on an invariant-domain lemma stated without proof (p.7). Table 2 OCR is garbled for tau (value text '000000001112433819', p.33) and for nu; treat those entries as unverified.
The network framing (p.3, p.23) is not modeled: peer influence is mass action and no network data are used.
measures: Final counts of yes (Y), no (N), undecided (C) legislators, House and Senate.
Percent error against actual yes and no tallies (p.19-20).
Pass/fail classification of parameter sweeps and linear SVM decision boundaries (p.14-17).
Sensitivity of final C, Y, N and lobbyist counts L_F, L_A to 10% parameter changes (p.12-13, Fig 12).
references_of_note: [17] Meng and Rode 2019, 'The social cost of lobbying over climate policy', Nature Climate Change 9:472-476. Source of the firm-value lobbying framework and the ACESA lobbying effects cited in the Introduction (14% of expenditures; about 13% passage reduction, p.2).
[7] Fong 2020, 'Expertise, networks, and interpersonal influence in Congress', J. Politics 82(1). Cited as the source of the beta peer-influence rates (Table 2).
[14] Kim and Kunisky 2021, 'Mapping political communities: lobbying networks in legislative politics', Political Analysis 29(3). Lobbying-network reference (p.2).
[15] Lan and Shah 2013, 'Utilizing network analysis to model congressional voting behavior'. Network-based voting model reference (p.2).
[12] Hojnacki and Kimball 1998, 'Organized interests and the decision of whom to lobby in Congress', APSR 92(4). Cited as a source for the phi lobbying rates (Table 2).
[4] Baumgartner et al. 2014, 'Money, priorities, and stalemate', Election Law Journal 13(1). Source of psi = 0.47847 (Table 2).
[5] Bonica 2018, 'Inferring roll-call scores from campaign contributions using supervised machine learning', AJPS 62(4). Cited for the claim that donations may reflect ideology (p.20).
[19] Poole and Rosenthal 1985, 'A spatial model for legislative roll call analysis', AJPS 29(2). Spatial/ideal-point baseline (p.3).
[3] Bari, Brower and Davidson 2021, ICBDA. Transformer embedding plus campaign finance reaching over 90% roll-call prediction accuracy (p.3). Machine-learning vote-prediction comparator.
[21] Smith et al. 2012, 'Predicting congressional votes based on campaign finance data', ICMLA. Campaign-finance vote prediction (p.3).
[23] Ward 2004, 'Pressure politics: a game-theoretical investigation of lobbying', J. Theoretical Politics 16(1). Game-theoretic lobbying model (p.2).
[18] Nehama 2015, 'Complexity of optimal lobbying in threshold aggregation'. Optimization view of lobbying (p.2).
[16] Voteview roll-call database (Lewis et al.). Source of the alpha ideology-flow rates (Table 2).
[24] ProPublica Represent (Willis, McCartney, Merrill). Source of the lobbyist counts (Sec 2.4, p.9) and of nu (Table 2).

rel.summary_md:
Jacoby et al. (arXiv 2505.09617, 2025) model a legislature the way an epidemic model tracks a population. Each legislator sits in one of four compartments: not yet introduced (S), undecided centrist (C), yes (Y) or no (N). Undecided members move to Y or N through mass-action contact with members who have already decided. The extended model adds lobbyist counts and lobbying money (L_F, L_A, M_F, M_A) and drains campaign donations (I_F, I_A). Every parameter is fixed from earlier literature (Table 2); none is estimated. The model is checked against one bill, the 2009 Waxman-Markey vote (ACESA).

In the House, the baseline run gives 230 yes, 196 no and 9 undecided, against an actual 219 to 212. Adding donations moves 1 member. Adding lobbying resolves 8 more undecided members (231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided). The Senate barely changes. The analysis shows that the centrist-flow and centrist-lobbying parameters (M_LF, M_LA) drive the outcome. An SVM finds no clean pass/fail boundary. Widening the centrist ideology band from ±0.25 to ±0.35 reverses the House result.

For Paul's system this is weak evidence. Each chamber has one comparison point, every "effect" is the output of parameters the authors chose, and the paper's claim of accuracy within 5% does not hold against its own errors of 5.02%, 5.48% and 7.55%. Its useful content is structural, not empirical:
- Legislators who have already decided are treated as fixed, and only undecided members move. This matches the low PERS values for Champion and Opponent.
- Who counts as movable decides the result. The system already found the same thing when it swept PERS_NONE.
- The sensitivity harness does not sweep the flip model's WM/WP channel weights or the PERS table. The paper says centrist-flow parameters are the ones that matter, so those are the obvious next sweeps.

The lobbying-versus-donations contrast should not be imported into the flip model. It is a contrast between simulation runs, not an estimate. Its lobbyist counts also come from revolving-door staff, and project rules bar LDA as an edge or weight source (D-021).

bearings.paper_claim: Varying the centrist-flow parameters by 10% produces a wide spread of final C, Y and N counts. In the parameter-impact ranking, centrist-lobbying parameters (M_LF, M_LA) and tau rank high and initial compartment sizes rank low. Linear SVMs on 1000-sample sweeps find no clean pass/fail boundary in multi-parameter sweeps.
bearings.system_side: The receptivity sensitivity harness sweeps only receptivity constants: susc scale, prospect-theory multipliers, retiring factor and persona weight (VARIANTS). It grades each by top-20 overlap (ROBUST at 18 or more). The harness does not sweep the flip model's channel weights WM/WP (0.35/0.65) or the PERS persuadability table. The one centrist-like knob that has been swept, PERS_NONE, was swept by hand and recorded in a comment: top-20 overlap was 16/18/20/18/15 across 0.30-0.95, and total winnability ran from 149.5 to 245.8.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transfer is a method idea, not evidence. Jacoby's sensitivity comes from a well-mixed ODE model with literature-fixed parameters, and the system's flip model is a network-based ratio of saturating terms. What carries over is the diagnostic: the parameters that decide who is movable and how fast they move should be swept first. The pass/fail SVM is not needed, because top-k overlap already measures decision change. Any such sweep is a bound on the model, not validation (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Only undecided centrists (C) move. Committed Y and N legislators are absorbing states, and the equilibrium with all members undecided is unstable. Widening the centrist band on a -1 to 1 ideology scale from ±0.25 to ±0.35 reverses the House result so that no votes exceed yes votes.
bearings.system_side: PERS assigns committed tiers near-zero persuadability (Champion 0.10, Opponent 0.08) and middle tiers the highest (Highly Persuadable 0.65). Silent members get PERS_NONE 0.45, which covers about 60% of cells. Tiers are based on stance, not ideology.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the extremes being near-fixed only because its model assumes it; Y and N are absorbing by construction. It does not test an inverted-U. Its centrist group is defined by an unnamed ideology scale, while PERS is defined by CU stance tier, so the band result carries over only as a warning: how the movable set is defined can decide the outcome. The system's PERS_NONE sweep shows the same thing in the system itself. Evidence is a single bill (ACESA, 2009) at the federal level.

bearings.paper_claim: With literature-fixed parameters, adding donations to the House run moves 1 legislator (230 to 231 yes). Adding lobbying resolves 8 of the 9 undecided members (final 231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided). The authors conclude that lobbying sways undecided members more than donations do.
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), with a saturating FEC-money term weighted WM 0.35 and a peer-proximity term weighted WP 0.65. Money is treated as the minority channel. The model has no lobbying-contact channel; money means campaign receipts only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Directionally consistent with the claim that money moves votes little, but this is a contrast between simulation runs under chosen inputs, not an estimated effect. The firm-value inputs (rho_Y, rho_N, Delta pi) are not reported, the effect covers 8 of 435 members on one bill, and the lobbying input is a count of revolving-door lobbyists. The paper gives no basis for setting WM/WP or for adding a lobbying channel. Under D-021, LDA data cannot become an edge or weight term.

bearings.paper_claim: Campaign donations alone move one House member out of 435 (from 9 undecided to 8) and leave the Senate essentially unchanged. The authors note that donations may reflect ideology rather than buy influence (citing Bonica).
bearings.system_side: MAXSHIFT was cut from 40 to 18 on the premise that money moves positions little, so money-triggered defections are rare and need about a sixth of a member's receipts. Champion and Opponent tiers are immune.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a consistency check, not a calibration. The donation effect in the paper is a model output from literature parameters (I_F, I_A taken from Meng and Rode), not an observed shift. It is weaker than the experimental and null-result literature already cited at money_response.py:15.

gaps_exposed: The receptivity sensitivity harness sweeps only receptivity constants (fec/members/receptivity_sensitivity.py:93-103). It does not sweep the flip model's WM/WP channel split (flip_model.py:21) or the PERS tier values (moneyball_core.py:564-568), which are the system's equivalents of the centrist-flow parameters the paper finds dominant. PERS_NONE was swept once by hand and the result exists only as a code comment.

The system has no test of how the movable set is defined. PERS assigns persuadability by stance-tier label, and nothing measures how much targeting changes when tier cutpoints move. The paper's centrist-band reversal (±0.25 to ±0.35) shows that the band definition alone can decide the outcome.

The paper's whole premise is a timeline of how members move from undecided to decided, and the system has no outcome check of that kind. The prospective contract (H1/H2) is the planned check, but its F5 power gate is underpowered (72 of the 150 required new-event members).
flags: The lobbying-versus-donations finding must not be used to add a lobbying channel or weight to the flip model. Its lobbying input is a count of ACESA-related lobbyists, and LDA is an identity source only, not an edge or weight source (D-021).
The paper's lobbyist series counts former federal employees, i.e. revolving-door staff (Sec 2.4, p.9). Any summary must not describe those ties with influence language.

The paper's headline accuracy claim ('within 5%', p.3) is contradicted by its own errors (5.02% and 7.55% at baseline; 5.48% yes with lobbying). If quoted, name the window and denominator: one bill (ACESA 2009), House N=435, one comparison per chamber, parameters not estimated.
Any SVM boundary or parameter-impact ranking from the paper describes the model, not legislators. If adapted here, the result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The paper frames lobbying as influence spreading through a network (p.3), but the model is well-mixed mass action with no network. Do not cite it as network-diffusion evidence for the cascade kernel.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's highlights accurately reflect what the paper reports: lobbying moves undecided members more than donations do, outcomes are highly sensitive to centrist-flow parameters, and centrists shift under outside pressure. His notes do not record how thin the evidence is. It is one bill, every parameter is fixed from earlier literature, the lobbying effect is 8 legislators resolved out of 435, and the paper's 5% accuracy claim fails against its own numbers. Read correctly, the paper is consistent with the system's stance that money buys access more than votes (WM 0.35 < WP 0.65; MAXSHIFT 18) and with near-fixed extremes in PERS. It gives no basis for the specific values. Pairing it in his notes with Paul's ROI enthusiasm overstates it. His sensitivity highlight is the most actionable part and is not stale: the system bounds receptivity constants but has not swept its own centrist-flow analogues (WM/WP and the PERS tiers). The lobbying channel he highlighted (green) cannot be built from LDA under D-021.

related.why: Jacoby cites Bonica (the 2018 roll-call inference paper) for the claim that donations may reflect ideology, not influence (p.20). The 2013 Bonica paper is Paul's on-disk anchor for that ideological-money reading.

Kalla and Broockman provide experimental evidence that money buys access. Jacoby's finding that donations barely move votes is a simulated parallel with no causal design, and Kalla is the stronger basis for the flip model's WM < WP.
Jacoby cites Kim and Kunisky's lobbying networks [14] as network-framing context, but the network is not modeled. Kim and Kunisky is the actual network treatment.
Jacoby defines centrists by an ideology band and cites NOMINATE and Voteview for the alpha ideology-flow rates. The band-width reversal depends on that ideal-point scale.

Jacoby's sensitivity runs are deterministic sweeps of 1000 samples. Monte Carlo practice, which the system already uses via common random numbers, is the stochastic extension the authors say they lack (p.22).

Furnas et al. separate lobbying from PAC spending at the organization level and find low overlap. Jacoby's lobbying-versus-donations split rests on parameter choices, not on data that separates the two channels.
